messages.content:
You check whether a set of acceptance criteria still asks for what a person asked for.
Agents write acceptance criteria from a person's request, and they tend to rewrite it into
something easier to build: a word like "graph" or "across documents" disappears and nothing
notices. Your job is to notice.

Step 1. Split every quote under ASKED_BY into its distinct requirements: each separate thing
the delivered outcome must be, do or show. Split finely: "a shared map of every store that
staff can filter and print" is five requirements (a map; shared; every store; can be
filtered; can be printed). Keep the person's own nouns: a requirement named "map" stays
"map", never "list" or "view". For each requirement give:
  - id: R1, R2, ... in order;
  - requirement: a short name in the person's own words (2 to 6 words);
  - quote: the exact words from the quote that state it, copied character for character
    (keep their typos);
  - asked_by_index: the 1-based number of the ASKED_BY quote it comes from;
  - kind: "outcome" (something the delivered thing must be or do), "constraint" (a rule about
    how it is shown or built that a criterion can still check), or "process" (a statement
    about how the planning work or the acceptance criteria themselves are written, which no
    demonstration of the outcome could show). Use "process" only when no working interface
    could ever demonstrate it.
When two quotes state the same requirement, list it once and quote the clearer one.

Step 2. For each requirement, decide which criteria cover it. A criterion covers a
requirement only when its criterion, demonstration or expected result would fail if the
requirement were not met. A criterion that is merely compatible with the requirement, or
that is about something nearby, does not cover it. For example a criterion "open the store
page and see every store's address" does not cover "map": a list of addresses passes it. List the
covering criterion ids, possibly none, and say why in one sentence. Then give the extent:
"full" when the listed criteria together would fail for any way of not meeting the
requirement; "partial" when they check only one part or one case of it, so something that
misses the rest still passes (say in "missing" what is left unasked); "none" when no
criterion covers it.

Step 3. If a requirement is covered by no criterion, check DEFERRALS. A requirement is
deferred only when a deferral's words, said by the person, approve leaving that requirement
out for now. Give the deferral's number, or 0 when none applies. Never treat an agent's note,
a plan or a criterion's own wording as a deferral.

Step 4. For each requirement of kind "outcome", say whether the OUTCOME line keeps it, in
substance, and why. An outcome line that says "staff look up any store" does not keep
"map", "filter" or "print".

Be strict and literal. Judge only from the text given.

ASKED_BY (the person's own words):

1. Brian, 2026-10-28: <<<ok my guess is that you hjave been fixing symptoms not root problems.the rpobelm i assuem si wiht our susbtrate and world generating process and world valdiating rpocess?>>>

2. Brian, 2026-10-28: <<<this "- Root fix: add a few built-in move types where the engine keeps the books: transfer / exchange / transform" seems to me liek it destorys the whol e potin of what we are doing. but maybe im missing something. what do you mean the substrate doesnt know what moeny is? the llm generating it surely does.>>>

3. Brian, 2026-10-28: <<<yes lets make it companhy plannign complaint>>>


OUTCOME (the agent's one-line restatement):
<<<A visitor builds a world on the World Builder whose moves the AI still writes freely, whose own bookkeeping laws the AI declares from what it knows about that kind of world (buying means paying, goods have to be made), whose engine refuses and records any step that breaks them, naming the law, and whose rules an independent review reads against the description, so the root problems in the substrate, the world-generating process and the world-validating process are fixed rather than one symptom at a time.>>>

CRITERIA:

[A1] 
  criterion: When I build a world, the build record shows that world's own bookkeeping laws in plain words, and they are right for that world: the AI that designs it uses what it knows (that buying means paying, that pencils have to be made).
  demonstration: (1) Open the World Builder. (2) Paste the pencil description and press Create simulation. (3) When the build finishes, open the build record and read the Laws list. 
  expected: A short list of sentences in the pencil world's own words, such as "Pencils are made only by assembling them and used up only by a customer" and "A sale moves pencils to the buyer and cash to the seller", each naming things and moves that appear elsewhere on the page, and each one true of the world the description describes.

[A2] 
  criterion: The engine itself keeps each world's declared laws: a move, or a knock-on effect it sets off, that breaks one is refused, and the page says which law it broke.
  demonstration: (1) Open the World Builder's replay of the saved pencil13 world, re-built in S2 so that the world design AI wrote its laws (the S2 report gives the link and shows the laws came from the model reply, not a person). (2) Go to round 8 and find the shop's buy-boxed-pencils move; read what the page says about it. (3) Open the S2 report's second replay, a world whose move sets off a knock-on effect that breaks a law (for example a fall that would destroy cash), and read that round. (4) Share the pencil13 replay, open the shared link in a new window, and go back to round 8. 
  expected: The purchase is marked refused (orange, with the word "refused") beside a law in plain words saying a purchase must move payment the other way; the shop's boxes and the factory's cash are unchanged that round. In the knock-on replay the move that set off the effect is refused the same way, the page names the knock-on effect that broke the law, and nothing from that moment is kept. The shared link shows the same refusal in the same round: the engine keeps it in the world's recorded history, with the moment that caused it.

[A3] 
  criterion: An independent review points out where the rules do not match my description, in my description's words.
  demonstration: (1) Open the build record of the saved pencil13 world reviewed in S3 (link given in the S3 report). (2) Open the review panel: it shows what the reviewer was given (the description, the laws and the rules, nothing else) and which model reviewed, next to the model that wrote the rules. (3) Read the Review findings list. 
  expected: The panel shows the reviewer got only the description, the laws and the rules, and a different model from the rules writer. Each finding names one rule and quotes the words of the description it was checked against; one finding says buy-boxed-pencils takes the boxes but pays the factory nothing.

[A4] 
  criterion: The pencil world I build runs with every sale paying for what it takes.
  demonstration: (1) Open the World Builder, paste the pencil description and press Create simulation. (2) Let the run play, then open any sale in the round list or the network view. 
  expected: Each sale moves pencils to the buyer and cash to the seller in the same step, including the shop buying boxes from the factory; the build record lists the laws and the review findings.

[A5] 
  criterion: Moves are still written freely in each world's own terms; there is no fixed menu of move types.
  demonstration: (1) Open the World Builder and build the pencil world; open its list of moves. (2) Build a kitchen description the same way and open its list of moves. 
  expected: Each world's moves carry its own names and effects (cut cedar, assemble pencils, sell a box; chop, plate, serve), and neither list shows built-in kinds such as transfer, exchange or transform.

[A6] 
  criterion: Descriptions the World Builder has never seen, of very different shapes and lengths, each build a world that keeps its own laws, with no code written for any of them.
  demonstration: (1) Open the World Builder and build each of four different descriptions in turn: the pencil supply chain, the airfield, a kitchen, and the long Waltzman scenario (people and organizations, not goods). (2) For each, open the build record's Laws and Review findings, then the run. (3) Open any refused step, and any sale or hand-over in the run. 
  expected: Each of the four worlds has laws naming its own things and moves (the Waltzman world may declare few or none, and says so); every refused step names the law it broke, including knock-on effects; every hand-over that a law pairs moves both sides; the review's findings quote that description's own words; all four builds finish.

[A7] 
  criterion: Mistakes in a world's rules are fixed at the root, in the engine, the world design and the review that every world shares, not by patches for one world or by a growing list of hand-written checks, one per mistake.
  demonstration: (1) Open a finished build record on the World Builder and read the panel that says what checked the rules. (2) Open the S4 table on this plan's review page: each retired hand-written check, the incident it was added for, and what catches that incident now. (3) On this plan's review page, open each finished slice's row: it lists, in plain words, what changed and where (the engine's law check, the world design's laws, the review), and whether any change names one world. 
  expected: The build record lists three kinds of checking only: the world's declared laws, the review's findings, and reports of what the test run saw. Each retired check in the S4 table points at a saved world where a law refusal or a review finding now catches its incident, and no new hand-written check was added for a new mistake. Every slice's changes sit in the parts all worlds share; none names pencils, the cafe or any other single world.


DEFERRALS:

none recorded

mappings.coverage_reason: A7 fails if changes name a single world, if hand-written checks accumulate, or if the build record shows more than the three shared checking types — all of which would expose symptom-patching rather than a root fix.
mappings.outcome_reason: OUTCOME closes with 'the root problems... are fixed rather than one symptom at a time', keeping this requirement.

mappings.coverage_reason: A2 fails if the engine (substrate) does not refuse law-breaking moves or knock-on effects; A7 fails if engine changes are absent from the shared parts listed in the S4 table.
mappings.outcome_reason: OUTCOME says 'the root problems in the substrate... are fixed', keeping this requirement.

mappings.coverage_reason: A1 fails if the build record's laws are wrong for the pencil world; A6 fails if any of the four structurally different worlds lacks laws that name its own things and moves.
mappings.outcome_reason: OUTCOME says 'the world-generating process... are fixed', keeping this requirement.

mappings.coverage_reason: A3 fails if the review panel does not show an independent reviewer finding rule-to-description mismatches, or if the reviewer was given anything beyond the description, laws and rules.
mappings.outcome_reason: OUTCOME says 'the world-validating process are fixed', keeping this requirement.

mappings.coverage_reason: A5 explicitly checks that neither world's move list shows built-in kinds such as transfer, exchange or transform; it fails if any such fixed type appears.
mappings.outcome_reason: Non-outcome kind: OUTCOME says 'moves the AI still writes freely', consistent with this constraint.

mappings.coverage_reason: A1 fails if the build record's laws are not true of the world (showing the LLM did not apply domain knowledge); A2 demonstration requires the S2 report to show the laws came from the model reply, not a person, so it fails if LLM authorship is absent.
mappings.outcome_reason: OUTCOME says 'the AI declares from what it knows about that kind of world (buying means paying, goods have to be made)', keeping this requirement.

mappings.coverage_reason: All criteria demonstrate software behavior; none tests whether the planning document itself follows the company planning format.
mappings.outcome_reason: Non-outcome kind: the OUTCOME line describes the delivered software and does not speak to the planning document's format.
